1570 | ):
1571 |     """Format a fixed width table for pretty printing.
1572 | 
1573 |     >>> print(tabulate([[1, 2.34], [-56, "8.999"], ["2", "10001"]]))
1574 |     ---  ---------
1575 |       1      2.34
1576 |     -56      8.999
1577 |       2  10001
1578 |     ---  ---------
1579 | 
1580 |     The first required argument (`tabular_data`) can be a
1581 |     list-of-lists (or another iterable of iterables), a list of named
1582 |     tuples, a dictionary of iterables, an iterable of dictionaries,
1583 |     an iterable of dataclasses (Python 3.7+), a two-dimensional NumPy array,
1584 |     NumPy record array, or a Pandas' dataframe.
1585 | 
1586 | 
1587 |     Table headers
1588 |     -------------
1589 | 
1590 |     To print nice column headers, supply the second argument (`headers`):
1591 | 
1592 |       - `headers` can be an explicit list of column headers
1593 |       - if `headers="firstrow"`, then the first row of data is used
1594 |       - if `headers="keys"`, then dictionary keys or column indices are used
1595 | 
1596 |     Otherwise a headerless table is produced.
1597 | 
1598 |     If the number of headers is less than the number of columns, they
1599 |     are supposed to be names of the last columns. This is consistent
1600 |     with the plain-text format of R and Pandas' dataframes.
1601 | 
1602 |     >>> print(tabulate([["sex","age"],["Alice","F",24],["Bob","M",19]],
1603 |     ...       headers="firstrow"))
1604 |            sex      age
1605 |     -----  -----  -----
1606 |     Alice  F         24
1607 |     Bob    M         19
1608 | 
1609 |     By default, pandas.DataFrame data have an additional column called
1610 |     row index. To add a similar column to all other types of data,
1611 |     use `showindex="always"` or `showindex=True`. To suppress row indices
1612 |     for all types of data, pass `showindex="never" or `showindex=False`.
1613 |     To add a custom row index column, pass `showindex=some_iterable`.
1614 | 
1615 |     >>> print(tabulate([["F",24],["M",19]], showindex="always"))
1616 |     -  -  --
1617 |     0  F  24
1618 |     1  M  19
1619 |     -  -  --
1620 | 
1621 | 
1622 |     Column alignment
1623 |     ----------------
1624 | 
1625 |     `tabulate` tries to detect column types automatically, and aligns
1626 |     the values properly. By default it aligns decimal points of the
1627 |     numbers (or flushes integer numbers to the right), and flushes
1628 |     everything else to the left. Possible column alignments
1629 |     (`numalign`, `stralign`) are: "right", "center", "left", "decimal"
1630 |     (only for `numalign`), and None (to disable alignment).
1631 | 
1632 | 
1633 |     Table formats
1634 |     -------------
1635 | 
1636 |     `intfmt` is a format specification used for columns which
1637 |     contain numeric data without a decimal point. This can also be
1638 |     a list or tuple of format strings, one per column.
1639 | 
1640 |     `floatfmt` is a format specification used for columns which
1641 |     contain numeric data with a decimal point. This can also be
1642 |     a list or tuple of format strings, one per column.
1643 | 
1644 |     `None` values are replaced with a `missingval` string (like
1645 |     `floatfmt`, this can also be a list of values for different
1646 |     columns):
1647 | 
1648 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 1, None],
1649 |     ...                 ["eggs", 42, 3.14],
1650 |     ...                 ["other", None, 2.7]], missingval="?"))
1651 |     -----  --  ----
1652 |     spam    1  ?
1653 |     eggs   42  3.14
1654 |     other   ?  2.7
1655 |     -----  --  ----
1656 | 
1657 |     Various plain-text table formats (`tablefmt`) are supported:
1658 |     'plain', 'simple', 'grid', 'pipe', 'orgtbl', 'rst', 'mediawiki',
1659 |     'latex', 'latex_raw', 'latex_booktabs', 'latex_longtable' and tsv.
1660 |     Variable `tabulate_formats`contains the list of currently supported formats.
1661 | 
1662 |     "plain" format doesn't use any pseudographics to draw tables,
1663 |     it separates columns with a double space:
1664 | 
1665 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 41.9999], ["eggs", "451.0"]],
1666 |     ...                 ["strings", "numbers"], "plain"))
1667 |     strings      numbers
1668 |     spam         41.9999
1669 |     eggs        451
1670 | 
1671 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 41.9999], ["eggs", "451.0"]], tablefmt="plain"))

1673 |     eggs  451

1567 |     maxcolwidths=None,
1568 |     rowalign=None,
1569 |     maxheadercolwidths=None,
1570 | ):
1571 |     """Format a fixed width table for pretty printing.
1572 | 
1573 |     >>> print(tabulate([[1, 2.34], [-56, "8.999"], ["2", "10001"]]))
1574 |     ---  ---------
1575 |       1      2.34
1576 |     -56      8.999
1577 |       2  10001
1578 |     ---  ---------
1579 | 
1580 |     The first required argument (`tabular_data`) can be a
1581 |     list-of-lists (or another iterable of iterables), a list of named
1582 |     tuples, a dictionary of iterables, an iterable of dictionaries,
1583 |     an iterable of dataclasses (Python 3.7+), a two-dimensional NumPy array,
1584 |     NumPy record array, or a Pandas' dataframe.
1585 | 
1586 | 
1587 |     Table headers
1588 |     -------------
1589 | 
1590 |     To print nice column headers, supply the second argument (`headers`):
1591 | 
1592 |       - `headers` can be an explicit list of column headers
1593 |       - if `headers="firstrow"`, then the first row of data is used
1594 |       - if `headers="keys"`, then dictionary keys or column indices are used
1595 | 
1596 |     Otherwise a headerless table is produced.
1597 | 
1598 |     If the number of headers is less than the number of columns, they
1599 |     are supposed to be names of the last columns. This is consistent
1600 |     with the plain-text format of R and Pandas' dataframes.
1601 | 
1602 |     >>> print(tabulate([["sex","age"],["Alice","F",24],["Bob","M",19]],
1603 |     ...       headers="firstrow"))
1604 |            sex      age
1605 |     -----  -----  -----
1606 |     Alice  F         24
1607 |     Bob    M         19
1608 | 
1609 |     By default, pandas.DataFrame data have an additional column called
1610 |     row index. To add a similar column to all other types of data,
1611 |     use `showindex="always"` or `showindex=True`. To suppress row indices
1612 |     for all types of data, pass `showindex="never" or `showindex=False`.
1613 |     To add a custom row index column, pass `showindex=some_iterable`.
1614 | 
1615 |     >>> print(tabulate([["F",24],["M",19]], showindex="always"))
1616 |     -  -  --
1617 |     0  F  24
1618 |     1  M  19
1619 |     -  -  --
1620 | 
1621 | 
1622 |     Column alignment
1623 |     ----------------
1624 | 
1625 |     `tabulate` tries to detect column types automatically, and aligns
1626 |     the values properly. By default it aligns decimal points of the
1627 |     numbers (or flushes integer numbers to the right), and flushes
1628 |     everything else to the left. Possible column alignments
1629 |     (`numalign`, `stralign`) are: "right", "center", "left", "decimal"
1630 |     (only for `numalign`), and None (to disable alignment).
1631 | 
1632 | 
1633 |     Table formats
1634 |     -------------
1635 | 
1636 |     `intfmt` is a format specification used for columns which
1637 |     contain numeric data without a decimal point. This can also be
1638 |     a list or tuple of format strings, one per column.
1639 | 
1640 |     `floatfmt` is a format specification used for columns which
1641 |     contain numeric data with a decimal point. This can also be
1642 |     a list or tuple of format strings, one per column.
1643 | 
1644 |     `None` values are replaced with a `missingval` string (like
1645 |     `floatfmt`, this can also be a list of values for different
1646 |     columns):
1647 | 
1648 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 1, None],
1649 |     ...                 ["eggs", 42, 3.14],
1650 |     ...                 ["other", None, 2.7]], missingval="?"))
1651 |     -----  --  ----
1652 |     spam    1  ?
1653 |     eggs   42  3.14
1654 |     other   ?  2.7
1655 |     -----  --  ----
1656 | 
1657 |     Various plain-text table formats (`tablefmt`) are supported:
1658 |     'plain', 'simple', 'grid', 'pipe', 'orgtbl', 'rst', 'mediawiki',
1659 |     'latex', 'latex_raw', 'latex_booktabs', 'latex_longtable' and tsv.
1660 |     Variable `tabulate_formats`contains the list of currently supported formats.
1661 | 
1662 |     "plain" format doesn't use any pseudographics to draw tables,
1663 |     it separates columns with a double space:
1664 | 
1665 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 41.9999], ["eggs", "451.0"]],
1666 |     ...                 ["strings", "numbers"], "plain"))
1667 |     strings      numbers
1668 |     spam         41.9999
1669 |     eggs        451
1670 | 
1671 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 41.9999], ["eggs", "451.0"]], tablefmt="plain"))

1673 |     eggs  451

1676 | 
1677 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 41.9999], ["eggs", "451.0"]],
1678 |     ...                 ["strings", "numbers"], "simple"))
